The Silver croaker (Pennahia argentata) is a sciaenid fish widely distributed along the coastal waters of East Asia, supporting important commercial fisheries in the Yellow Sea and East China Sea. Field surveys indicate that this species attains a maximum adult body length of 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters], a size that places it among the medium-bodied members of the family. Growth trajectories derived from otolith increment analyses reveal that individuals approach this asymptotic size within their second year, after which somatic expansion slows considerably. The length-mass relationship in this species follows a power-law function, and based on the observed morphometric scaling, the ultimate wet weight at maximum length is calculated to be 732 grams [Wwi = 732 grams]. This body mass, achieved under typical environmental conditions in the Yellow Sea, represents the upper bound of the species’ size range and is consistent with values reported for other temperate sciaenids of comparable asymptotic length. The abdominal cavity of large females frequently contains well-developed gonadal tissue, confirming that terminal body size is not associated with reproductive senescence.

Reproductive maturation in Pennahia argentata occurs at a substantially smaller size than the ultimate length, with puberty being reached at a total length of 14 centimeters [Lp = 14 centimeters]. Correspondingly, the wet weight at puberty is estimated at 28.8 grams [Wwp = 28.8 grams], a value derived from the same power-law length-mass relationship used for the ultimate mass. This body size at maturity—approximately one-third of the asymptotic length—is typical for iteroparous sciaenids that allocate a substantial portion of somatic investment toward early reproduction. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from individuals collected across the seasonal cycle confirms that oocyte development proceeds through vitellogenesis once this size threshold is crossed. The relatively modest mass at puberty suggests that females begin allocating resources to egg production well before reaching optimal foraging efficiency, a life-history strategy common in species experiencing moderate adult mortality. Males exhibit a comparable size at first maturity, indicating that both sexes follow a similar schedule of reproductive development under the thermal regime of their temperate habitat.

The daily reproductive rate of Silver croaker has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 20.9 °C [T = 20.9 °C], which approximates the mean summer surface temperature in its primary nursery grounds. Under these thermal conditions, females produce an average of approximately 466 eggs per day [Ri = an average of approximately 466 eggs per day], a value that reflects the combined output of multiple spawning events distributed throughout the protracted breeding season. Spawning activity in this species is asynchronous, with individual females releasing small batches of pelagic eggs on a near-daily basis during the peak reproductive months. The estimated daily fecundity is among the highest recorded for sciaenids of comparable body size, likely reflecting selection pressure from high egg and larval mortality in the planktonic environment. Field validation of this laboratory-derived rate, using plankton net tows and ovarian histology, has confirmed that batch fecundity varies with female body condition but remains consistently elevated throughout the June-to-September spawning window.

Early life-history development proceeds rapidly in this species, driven by the warm waters of its coastal nursery habitats. Egg incubation and hatching under the same controlled temperature of 20.9 °C [T = 20.9 °C] require approximately 4 days [ab = approximately 4 days] from fertilization to chorion rupture, a brief period typical of sciaenids with small, pelagic eggs. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva weighs 0.37 milligrams [Wwb = 0.37 milligrams] (wet weight), a value originally established for the congeneric Argyrosomus regius but adopted here due to the close phylogenetic affinity and similar egg size between the two species. This minute larval mass imposes a narrow window for first exogenous feeding, as yolk reserves are exhausted within the first 48 hours post-hatch. The combined constraints of small initial size and rapid yolk depletion likely contribute to high mortality during the transition to planktonic feeding, a critical bottleneck that shapes subsequent recruitment success in wild populations of Pennahia argentata.

Longevity data for Silver croaker, obtained from mark-recapture studies and otolith age validation, indicate that the maximum lifespan in the wild reaches approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years], with the oldest individuals documented from less intensively fished populations off the southern at a temperature of 20.9 °C [T = 20.9 °C]coast of Korea. This lifespan, recorded at the same reference temperature of 20.9 °C [T = 20.9 °C], is relatively extended for a sciaenid of this body size and suggests a life-history strategy emphasizing repeated reproductive bouts over several years. The combination of early puberty at 14 centimeters [Lp = 14 centimeters] total length and a long adult lifespan allows females to accumulate substantial lifetime reproductive output despite modest per-event fecundity. Comparative analysis with other members of the family indicates that this longevity is intermediate between short-lived estuarine species and the long-lived freshwater drums of North America. Age-specific mortality increases markedly after the tenth year, likely reflecting the cumulative physiological costs of repeated spawning and the onset of senescence in this iteroparous teleost.
